It united all aliʻi nui under one peaceful government
practice.explain: European trade introduced new weapons like muskets and cannon that were not equally available to every chief, giving whichever aliʻi nui secured better access a real military edge over rivals, an advantage Kamehameha would later exploit.

practice.q: Which rivalry in the 1770s and 1780s reshaped island alliances just before Kamehameha's rise?
choices: Kamehameha versus Liliʻuokalani
Kalaniʻōpuʻu of Hawaiʻi Island versus Kahekili of Maui
Cook versus the British Navy
Kaʻahumanu versus Kauikeaouli
practice.explain: The recurring conflicts between Kalaniʻōpuʻu, aliʻi nui of Hawaiʻi Island, and Kahekili, aliʻi nui of Maui, weakened both sides and reshaped alliances right before Kamehameha began his rise to power.

units.title: Unification and the Hawaiian Kingdom
units.summary: How Kamehameha I unified the islands into a single kingdom, how the ancient kapu system ended, and how the kingdom modernized under his successors.

lessons.title: Kamehameha I and the Unification of the Islands
lessons.intro: Starting as one ambitious chief among many on Hawaiʻi Island, Kamehameha used superior weapons, shrewd alliances, and a willingness to accept peaceful surrender when conquest wasn't necessary to become, for the first time in history, the sole ruler of all the major Hawaiian Islands.

sections.heading: Consolidating Hawaiʻi Island and Conquering Maui and Oʻahu
body: Kamehameha, a chief from Hawaiʻi Island, spent much of the 1780s and early 1790s consolidating control over his home island before turning his ambitions toward the other islands, acquiring Western weapons, cannon, muskets, and even a small number of foreign military advisors, through trade relationships with visiting ships, giving his forces a real technological edge over rivals still relying primarily on traditional weapons. He invaded Maui in 1790, and after also gaining ground against Oʻahu forces, fought his most decisive battle at the Battle of Nuʻuanu in 1795.

At Nuʻuanu, Kamehameha's forces, using cannon transported ashore and superior numbers, drove Oʻahu's defenders back through Nuʻuanu Valley until many were forced over the sheer cliffs of the Nuʻuanu Pali, a battle that gave Kamehameha effective control of Oʻahu and left him in command of every major island except Kauaʻi and Niʻihau.

sections.heading: Kauaʻi's Peaceful Cession and a Unified Kingdom
body: Kamehameha attempted invasions of Kauaʻi in 1796 and again in 1804, but both were turned back, the first by rough seas and the second by a devastating epidemic (likely typhoid or cholera) that struck his assembled invasion force before it could depart, sparing Kauaʻi from a third military campaign. Rather than continuing to risk a costly invasion, Kamehameha negotiated instead.

In 1810, Kauaʻi's aliʻi nui, Kaumualiʻi, agreed to formally cede control of Kauaʻi and Niʻihau to Kamehameha peacefully, in exchange for retaining a degree of local authority over his home island, completing the unification of all the major Hawaiian Islands under one ruler for the first time in history, and establishing Kamehameha as founder of the Hawaiian Kingdom.

example.problem: Explain why Kamehameha's final acquisition of Kauaʻi in 1810 came through a peaceful, negotiated cession rather than a third military invasion, given that he had already conquered every other major island by force.
steps: Kamehameha had already attempted two separate invasions of Kauaʻi, in 1796 and 1804, and both failed due to factors outside his control, rough seas and a devastating epidemic within his own invasion force, showing that conquering Kauaʻi militarily carried real risk and uncertain cost.

By 1810, Kamehameha had already secured control of every other major island, so continuing to seek a costly, uncertain third invasion of Kauaʻi offered less additional benefit relative to the risk than negotiating peacefully would.

Kaumualiʻi, facing a much more powerful unified rival controlling the rest of the islands, had strong incentive to accept a negotiated cession that let him keep some local authority, rather than risk losing everything in a war he was increasingly unlikely to win.
example.answer: After two failed invasions showed the real cost and risk of conquering Kauaʻi by force, and with Kamehameha already controlling every other island, both sides had strong incentive to accept a peaceful cession in 1810 instead of a third costly military campaign.

keyTerms.def: An 1795 battle in which Kamehameha's forces defeated Oʻahu's defenders, driving many over the Nuʻuanu Pali cliffs.
The aliʻi nui of Kauaʻi who peacefully ceded the island to Kamehameha in 1810, completing Hawaiian unification.
The unified Hawaiian state founded by Kamehameha I after completing control of all major islands in 1810.

practice.q: What gave Kamehameha's forces a decisive edge over rival chiefs during unification?
choices: A much larger population than any rival island
Western weapons, including cannon and muskets, acquired through trade with visiting ships
Support from the Persian Empire
The invention of the peleleu war canoe
practice.explain: Kamehameha's access to Western weapons and advisors through trade relationships with visiting ships gave his forces a real technological advantage over rivals relying primarily on traditional weapons.

practice.q: What happened at the Battle of Nuʻuanu in 1795?
choices: Kamehameha was defeated and retreated to Hawaiʻi Island
Kamehameha's forces drove Oʻahu's defenders back, many over the Nuʻuanu Pali cliffs, securing control of Oʻahu
Kauaʻi was conquered for the first time
Captain Cook was killed
practice.explain: At Nuʻuanu, Kamehameha's forces, aided by cannon and superior numbers, decisively defeated Oʻahu's defenders, driving many over the cliffs of the Nuʻuanu Pali and securing control of the island.

practice.q: How did Kamehameha ultimately gain control of Kauaʻi?
choices: A third successful military invasion in 1810
A peaceful cession negotiated with Kaumualiʻi in 1810 after two failed invasions
Kauaʻi was never brought under Kamehameha's control
Kauaʻi surrendered immediately after the Battle of Nuʻuanu
practice.explain: After two failed invasion attempts, Kamehameha secured Kauaʻi and Niʻihau through a peaceful 1810 agreement in which Kaumualiʻi ceded control while retaining some local authority.

practice.q: Why might Kaumualiʻi have preferred a negotiated cession over continued resistance in 1810?
choices: He had no interest in retaining any authority
Facing a unified rival controlling every other island, negotiation let him keep some local authority rather than risk losing everything
Kamehameha had no army left by 1810
Kauaʻi had already been conquered by a foreign power
practice.explain: With Kamehameha already controlling all other islands, Kaumualiʻi had strong incentive to negotiate a cession that preserved some of his local authority rather than risk total loss in a war he was unlikely to win.

lessons.title: The End of the Kapu System
lessons.intro: Just months after Kamehameha's death, his son and widow made a decision that would have been unthinkable under the old order: sitting down together at a public feast to deliberately break one of the most fundamental kapu of all, and in doing so, they dismantled the religious system that had structured Hawaiian life for centuries.

sections.heading: Kamehameha's Death and a Fragile Succession
body: Kamehameha I died in 1819, leaving the kingdom to his son Liholiho, who took the name Kamehameha II, but real power was shared in practice with Kaʻahumanu, one of Kamehameha's widows and a formidable political figure, who was given the specially created role of kuhina nui (a position combining elements of co-ruler and regent) to help guide the young, less politically experienced Liholiho.

Kaʻahumanu had long chafed against certain restrictions of the kapu system, particularly the ʻai kapu rules that strictly forbade men and women from eating together and barred women from eating certain foods considered sacred to male gods, and she saw Kamehameha's death as an opportunity to challenge a system that had begun to feel, to some of the political elite, increasingly out of step with the changing world Hawaiʻi now faced.

sections.heading: ʻAi Noa: Breaking the Eating Kapu
body: In late 1819, only months after Kamehameha's death, Liholiho, urged on by Kaʻahumanu and the dowager queen Keōpūolani, publicly sat down and ate together with women at a large feast, deliberately and visibly violating the ʻai kapu in an event historians call ʻai noa ("free eating"). Because kapu violations were traditionally believed to provoke swift divine punishment, and none followed this dramatic public act, the event effectively demonstrated to observers that the kapu system's sacred authority could be broken without consequence.

Following ʻai noa, Liholiho ordered the destruction of heiau (temples) and religious images across the islands, formally ending the traditional kapu-based state religious system just as the first American Protestant missionaries were arriving in Hawaiʻi in 1820, leaving a striking religious vacuum that Christianity would move to fill in the years that followed.

example.problem: Explain why the public, deliberate nature of the ʻai noa feast in 1819, rather than a private or accidental kapu violation, was so important to its effect on ending the wider kapu system.
steps: The entire kapu system rested on the belief that violations would provoke visible divine punishment, so the system's authority depended on people continuing to believe this consequence was real and would actually occur.

By making the violation public and highly visible, involving the king himself and prominent chiefs eating together with women in front of many witnesses, the event created a shared, undeniable observation that everyone present could see: no immediate divine punishment followed.

Because so many people witnessed this outcome together at once, the traditional belief that kapu violations brought swift consequences was publicly and simultaneously discredited in a way a private, unnoticed violation never could have achieved, undermining the system's authority across society all at once.
example.answer: The public nature of ʻai noa let a large number of people simultaneously witness that no divine punishment followed the violation, discrediting the kapu system's core claim in a visible, shared way that a private violation could never have accomplished.

keyTerms.def: Kamehameha I's son and successor, who presided over the 1819 breaking of the eating kapu.
A powerful widow of Kamehameha I who served as kuhina nui and helped orchestrate the end of the kapu system.
A specially created co-ruler or regent position in the Hawaiian Kingdom, first held by Kaʻahumanu.
"Free eating," the 1819 event in which Liholiho publicly ate with women, deliberately breaking the eating kapu.
Traditional Hawaiian temples, many of which were ordered destroyed following the end of the kapu system in 1819.

practice.q: What role did Kaʻahumanu hold after Kamehameha I's death?
choices: Kuhina nui, a co-ruler or regent position guiding the young Liholiho
Sole monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom
High priestess of the ʻai kapu system
Governor of Kauaʻi
practice.explain: Kaʻahumanu was given the specially created role of kuhina nui, functioning as a co-ruler or regent alongside Kamehameha I's young successor, Liholiho.

practice.q: What was the ʻai kapu?
choices: A restriction on Hawaiian voyaging
A rule forbidding men and women from eating together and restricting certain foods to men
A tax on farmed goods
A ceremony honoring Captain Cook
practice.explain: The ʻai kapu strictly forbade men and women from eating together and reserved certain sacred foods for men, one of the central restrictions of the traditional kapu system.

practice.q: Why was the public nature of the 1819 ʻai noa feast so significant?
choices: It had no real significance beyond a private family meal
It let many witnesses simultaneously see that no divine punishment followed the violation, discrediting the kapu system's authority
It was kept secret from the general population
It only affected Kauaʻi
practice.explain: Because the kapu system's authority depended on belief in swift divine punishment for violations, publicly demonstrating that no punishment followed undermined that belief across society at once, rather than in a private, unnoticed way.

practice.q: What happened to Hawaiian temples (heiau) after ʻai noa?
choices: They were preserved unchanged
Liholiho ordered many destroyed, formally ending the kapu-based state religion
They were converted into Christian churches immediately
They were relocated to Kauaʻi
practice.explain: Following ʻai noa, Liholiho ordered the destruction of heiau and religious images, formally dismantling the kapu-based state religious system just before American missionaries arrived in 1820.

lessons.title: The Kingdom Modernizes: Māhele and Constitution
lessons.intro: Within a single generation of Western contact, the Hawaiian Kingdom adopted a written constitution limiting royal power and radically restructured how land itself was owned, two sweeping changes meant to help Hawaiʻi survive as an independent, internationally recognized nation in a rapidly changing world.

sections.heading: Kamehameha III and the 1840 Constitution
body: Kamehameha III, who came to the throne as a child in 1825 and ruled until 1854, presided over the kingdom's most significant peacetime transformation. In 1840, he promulgated Hawaiʻi's first written constitution, establishing a legislature and formally limiting royal power, part of a broader strategy to have the Hawaiian Kingdom recognized internationally as a modern, sovereign nation capable of engaging as an equal with Western powers, an effort that succeeded when Great Britain and France jointly recognized Hawaiian independence in 1843.

This same period saw growing pressure from foreign residents and missionary advisors to reform Hawaiian land tenure, since under the traditional system land was not owned outright by individuals but held and managed collectively under chiefs and the crown, an arrangement foreign business interests found difficult to navigate for long-term investment such as sugar plantations.

sections.heading: The Great Māhele of 1848
body: In 1848, Kamehameha III enacted the Great Māhele, a sweeping land division that split all Hawaiian land into three broad categories, crown lands retained by the monarchy, government lands administered by the kingdom, and lands awarded to individual aliʻi, formally introducing the Western concept of private, individually owned land title into Hawaiʻi for the first time. A follow-up law, the Kuleana Act of 1850, allowed makaʻāinana commoners to also claim title to the small plots they actually farmed.

In practice, the Māhele disadvantaged many ordinary Hawaiians: unfamiliar with the new legal filing process, lacking cash to pay required survey and registration fees, and sometimes simply unaware their claims needed to be formally filed, many makaʻāinana never registered kuleana claims at all, while foreign and elite Hawaiian buyers steadily acquired large landholdings in the following decades, a land ownership shift with consequences still felt in Hawaiʻi today.

example.problem: Explain why the Great Māhele of 1848, despite including the Kuleana Act meant to let commoners claim land, ended up transferring much land into foreign and elite hands rather than securing broad land ownership among ordinary Hawaiians.
steps: The Māhele introduced an entirely new, unfamiliar legal concept, individually filed private land title, that required navigating written paperwork, surveys, and registration fees, none of which had ever been part of the traditional Hawaiian land system.

Many makaʻāinana lacked the cash needed to pay survey and filing fees, lacked familiarity with the new bureaucratic filing process, and in some cases were simply not aware that formally registering their claim was even necessary to secure ownership under the new system.

Because so many commoners never completed the registration process for lands they actually farmed, that land remained available for others, wealthier Hawaiian elites and foreign buyers with the resources and legal familiarity to navigate the new system, to acquire over the following decades.
example.answer: Because the Māhele's new land title process required cash, paperwork, and legal familiarity that many makaʻāinana lacked or were unaware of, most ordinary Hawaiians never registered land claims, leaving that land open for wealthier elites and foreign buyers to acquire instead.

keyTerms.def: The Hawaiian king (r. 1825–1854) who promulgated the 1840 Constitution and enacted the Great Māhele of 1848.
Hawaiʻi's first written constitution, establishing a legislature and formally limiting royal power.
An 1848 land division that introduced private, individually owned land title into Hawaiʻi for the first time.
An 1850 law allowing makaʻāinana commoners to claim title to the small plots of land they farmed.

practice.q: What did the 1840 Constitution establish in the Hawaiian Kingdom?
choices: A land redistribution program
A legislature and formal limits on royal power
The end of the monarchy entirely
A ban on foreign trade
practice.explain: Kamehameha III's 1840 Constitution created a legislature and formally limited royal authority, part of a broader effort to have Hawaiʻi recognized internationally as a modern sovereign nation.

practice.q: What was the Great Māhele of 1848?
choices: A war between Hawaiian chiefs
A land division introducing private, individually owned land title into Hawaiʻi
A treaty ending Hawaiian independence
A religious reform ending the kapu system
practice.explain: The Great Māhele divided Hawaiian land into crown, government, and aliʻi categories, introducing Western-style private land ownership for the first time.

practice.q: What was the purpose of the 1850 Kuleana Act?
choices: To ban commoners from owning any land
To let makaʻāinana commoners claim title to the plots of land they actually farmed
To give all land exclusively to foreign buyers
To restore the traditional kapu system
practice.explain: The Kuleana Act was meant to let ordinary Hawaiian commoners secure legal title to the land they farmed, following the broader land reforms of the Great Māhele.

practice.q: Why did many makaʻāinana fail to secure land titles under the Māhele and Kuleana Act?
choices: They were legally barred from filing any claims
Many lacked the cash for fees or familiarity with the new filing process, or were unaware registration was required
They preferred to remain landless by choice
The laws were never actually enacted
practice.explain: The new land title system required navigating unfamiliar paperwork, surveys, and fees, and many commoners lacked the resources or awareness to complete registration, while wealthier elites and foreign buyers acquired much of the unclaimed land.

units.title: Overthrow and Annexation
units.summary: How a wealthy planter and business class stripped the Hawaiian monarchy of power, overthrew the last Hawaiian queen, and secured U.S. annexation over the documented objection of most Native Hawaiians.

lessons.title: The Bayonet Constitution
lessons.intro: By the 1880s, a small class of mostly American and European sugar planters and businessmen had grown so economically powerful in Hawaiʻi that when King Kalākaua resisted their demands for greater political control, they simply forced him, at gunpoint, to sign away much of his own authority.

sections.heading: Sugar, the Reciprocity Treaty, and Growing Foreign Power
body: Hawaiʻi's sugar industry expanded enormously after the 1875 Reciprocity Treaty with the United States allowed Hawaiian sugar to enter the U.S. market duty-free, and this booming export economy concentrated growing wealth and influence in the hands of a small class of American and European planters and merchants, many organized informally through business and civic associations. King Kalākaua, elected to the throne in 1874 and known for reviving Hawaiian cultural practices like hula that missionary influence had suppressed, increasingly clashed with this business elite over control of government spending, appointments, and policy.

In 1887, a armed group calling itself the Hawaiian League, backed by an armed militia, confronted Kalākaua and, under implicit threat of violence or removal, forced him to sign a new constitution stripping the monarchy of most independent power and placing executive authority effectively under a cabinet controlled by the same business interests.

sections.heading: The Bayonet Constitution's Provisions
body: This 1887 document became known as the Bayonet Constitution because of the coercive, armed circumstances under which Kalākaua was forced to sign it, and it sharply restricted voting rights by imposing income and property ownership requirements that excluded most Native Hawaiians and Asian immigrant laborers from voting, while extending voting rights to many foreign resident businessmen who were not even Hawaiian citizens.

The Bayonet Constitution left the monarchy as a largely symbolic institution, with real governing power concentrated in a legislature and cabinet dominated by the same annexationist-leaning business elite who had forced its adoption, setting a direct precedent and template for an even more decisive move against the monarchy just six years later.

example.problem: Explain how the Bayonet Constitution's new voting requirements functioned to shift real political power away from Native Hawaiians and toward the foreign business elite that forced Kalākaua to sign it.
steps: The new constitution imposed income and property ownership requirements to vote, standards that excluded most Native Hawaiians and Asian immigrant laborers, who on average held less individual wealth and property than the foreign business class.

At the same time, the constitution extended voting rights to many foreign resident businessmen, including some who were not even Hawaiian citizens, specifically the group that benefited most from the sugar economy and had forced the constitution's adoption.

By excluding the group most likely to support the monarchy's continued authority while including the group seeking to limit it, the new voting rules shifted the electorate itself toward the business elite's interests, reinforcing their political control well beyond the original armed confrontation.
example.answer: By imposing wealth requirements that excluded most Native Hawaiians while extending voting rights to non-citizen foreign businessmen, the Bayonet Constitution reshaped the electorate itself to favor the business elite, entrenching their political power beyond just the initial forced signing.

keyTerms.def: A U.S.–Hawaiʻi trade agreement allowing Hawaiian sugar into the U.S. market duty-free, fueling the sugar industry's growth.
Hawaiian monarch (r. 1874–1891) known for reviving Hawaiian culture, forced to sign the Bayonet Constitution in 1887.
An armed group of mostly American and European businessmen that forced Kalākaua to sign the Bayonet Constitution.
An 1887 constitution forced on Kalākaua at gunpoint, stripping royal power and restricting voting rights by wealth.

practice.q: What economic development concentrated wealth among a small foreign business class in Hawaiʻi by the 1880s?
choices: The Great Māhele of 1848
The booming sugar export economy following the 1875 Reciprocity Treaty
The end of the kapu system in 1819
The arrival of Captain Cook in 1778
practice.explain: The 1875 Reciprocity Treaty let Hawaiian sugar enter the U.S. market duty-free, fueling a sugar export boom that concentrated wealth and power among mostly American and European planters and merchants.

practice.q: How did King Kalākaua come to sign the 1887 constitution?
choices: He proposed it voluntarily to modernize the government
He was forced to sign it under threat of an armed militia organized by the Hawaiian League
It was approved by a public referendum
He signed it while on a diplomatic trip abroad
practice.explain: The armed Hawaiian League confronted Kalākaua and forced him, under implicit threat of violence, to sign the constitution, which is why it became known as the Bayonet Constitution.

practice.q: How did the Bayonet Constitution's voting requirements shift political power in Hawaiʻi?
choices: They gave all residents equal voting rights
They excluded most Native Hawaiians and Asian immigrants through wealth requirements while including many foreign non-citizen businessmen
They abolished voting entirely
They gave voting rights only to the monarchy
practice.explain: Income and property requirements excluded most Native Hawaiians and Asian laborers from voting, while extending voting rights to foreign businessmen, some not even citizens, reshaping the electorate to favor the business elite.

practice.q: What was the overall effect of the Bayonet Constitution on the Hawaiian monarchy?
choices: It strengthened the monarchy's independent power
It reduced the monarchy to a largely symbolic role, with real power held by a business-dominated cabinet and legislature
It abolished the monarchy immediately
It transferred power to the U.S. federal government directly
practice.explain: The Bayonet Constitution left the monarchy largely symbolic, concentrating real governing power in a legislature and cabinet controlled by the same annexationist-leaning business elite who forced its adoption.

lessons.title: Queen Liliʻuokalani and the 1893 Overthrow
lessons.intro: When Queen Liliʻuokalani tried to restore powers stripped from the Hawaiian monarchy by proposing a new constitution, a group of businessmen, backed by the landing of armed United States Marines, overthrew her government within days, ending nearly a century of Hawaiian monarchy.

sections.heading: A Queen Seeks to Restore Royal Power
body: Liliʻuokalani succeeded her brother Kalākaua as monarch in 1891 and, responding to petitions from many Native Hawaiian subjects who wanted the monarchy's authority and voting rights restored, moved in January 1893 to promulgate a new constitution that would have reversed key provisions of the Bayonet Constitution. This announcement alarmed the same annexationist business elite, who formed a Committee of Safety and moved quickly to prevent the new constitution from taking effect.

On January 17, 1893, the Committee of Safety, with the support of John L. Stevens, the U.S. Minister to Hawaiʻi, and the landing of armed United States Marines from a Navy vessel stationed in Honolulu Harbor, ostensibly to protect American lives and property, declared the monarchy overthrown and proclaimed a Provisional Government.

sections.heading: Liliʻuokalani's Protest and the Path to Annexation
body: To avoid bloodshed, Liliʻuokalani yielded her authority not to the Provisional Government directly but to the government of the United States, explicitly under protest, trusting that the U.S. federal government would investigate and reverse what she and many others viewed as an illegal act carried out with unauthorized U.S. military support. President Grover Cleveland's own investigation, the Blount Report, later concluded the overthrow had indeed been illegal and that U.S. forces had improperly assisted it, and Cleveland refused to pursue annexation on those grounds.

Despite Cleveland's findings, the Provisional Government (reorganized in 1894 as the Republic of Hawaiʻi under Sanford Dole) refused to restore the monarchy, and Native Hawaiians overwhelmingly rejected annexation in the 1897 Kūʻē Petitions, over 21,000 signatures gathered against annexation, delivered to the U.S. Congress and credited with helping block ratification of an annexation treaty requiring a two-thirds Senate vote.

example.problem: Explain why Queen Liliʻuokalani chose to yield her authority specifically to the United States government rather than to the Provisional Government that had just overthrown her, and why that distinction mattered.
steps: Liliʻuokalani believed the overthrow had only succeeded because of the presence and implicit threat of armed United States Marines, meaning the Provisional Government's power rested on unauthorized U.S. military support rather than legitimate authority of its own.

By yielding specifically to the United States government rather than recognizing the Provisional Government directly, she was making a formal record that she considered the true responsible party to be the U.S., not a small local group acting on its own, and was preserving her legal claim that the takeover was illegitimate.

This distinction mattered practically because it gave her a basis to seek redress from the U.S. federal government itself, which she hoped, and which President Cleveland's own Blount Report later confirmed, would investigate and potentially reverse an action carried out with improper American military involvement.
example.answer: Liliʻuokalani yielded to the United States rather than the Provisional Government to formally place responsibility on the U.S. military support that made the overthrow possible, preserving her legal claim that the act was illegitimate and giving her a basis to seek its reversal, a claim Cleveland's Blount Report later validated.

keyTerms.def: The last monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom, overthrown in 1893 after attempting to restore royal authority.
The group of mostly American and European businessmen who organized and carried out the 1893 overthrow.
The U.S. Minister to Hawaiʻi who supported the 1893 overthrow and authorized the landing of U.S. Marines.
President Cleveland's 1893 investigation concluding the overthrow was illegal and improperly aided by U.S. forces.
1897 petitions signed by over 21,000 Native Hawaiians opposing annexation, helping block a Senate annexation treaty.

practice.q: What action by Queen Liliʻuokalani alarmed the businessmen who organized the 1893 overthrow?
choices: Her decision to abolish the sugar industry
Her attempt to promulgate a new constitution restoring monarchical power stripped by the Bayonet Constitution
Her alliance with a foreign European power
Her refusal to speak English publicly
practice.explain: Liliʻuokalani's move to introduce a new constitution reversing the Bayonet Constitution's restrictions alarmed the annexationist business elite, prompting them to form the Committee of Safety and act quickly.

practice.q: What U.S. involvement supported the 1893 overthrow?
choices: No United States involvement occurred
U.S. Minister John L. Stevens and the landing of armed U.S. Marines supported the overthrow
The U.S. Congress formally declared war on Hawaiʻi
The U.S. sent only diplomatic letters with no military presence
practice.explain: U.S. Minister John L. Stevens backed the Committee of Safety, and armed U.S. Marines landed from a Navy vessel in Honolulu Harbor, providing crucial support that helped the overthrow succeed.

practice.q: What did President Cleveland's Blount Report conclude?
choices: The overthrow was fully legal and justified
The overthrow was illegal and U.S. forces had improperly assisted it
Hawaiʻi should be annexed immediately
Queen Liliʻuokalani had staged the overthrow herself
practice.explain: The Blount Report, commissioned by President Cleveland, concluded that the 1893 overthrow was illegal and that U.S. military forces had improperly aided it, leading Cleveland to oppose annexation on those grounds.

practice.q: What was the significance of the 1897 Kūʻē Petitions?
choices: They supported annexation unanimously
Over 21,000 Native Hawaiian signatures opposing annexation helped block ratification of an annexation treaty in the Senate
They were a petition to restore the kapu system
They had no impact on U.S. policy
practice.explain: The Kūʻē Petitions demonstrated overwhelming Native Hawaiian opposition to annexation and are credited with helping deny the two-thirds Senate vote needed to ratify an annexation treaty.

lessons.title: Annexation and Becoming a U.S. Territory
lessons.intro: Twice blocked from ratifying a treaty of annexation by the Senate's two-thirds requirement and overwhelming Native Hawaiian opposition, the United States ultimately annexed Hawaiʻi anyway, using a legislative shortcut that needed only a simple majority in each chamber of Congress.

sections.heading: The Newlands Resolution
body: With a formal annexation treaty twice unable to secure the two-thirds Senate majority required, and amid rising U.S. strategic interest in Hawaiʻi as a Pacific naval and coaling station during the Spanish-American War, Congress instead passed the Newlands Resolution in July 1898, a joint resolution requiring only a simple majority in the House and Senate rather than the higher bar a treaty demanded. President William McKinley signed it, formally annexing Hawaiʻi as a U.S. territory despite the documented mass opposition expressed in the Kūʻē Petitions the previous year.

This procedural approach, using a joint resolution instead of a ratified treaty, remains legally controversial to some scholars and Native Hawaiian sovereignty advocates today, since the U.S. Constitution does not explicitly authorize acquiring foreign territory through a resolution requiring only simple majorities rather than the treaty process's higher constitutional threshold.

sections.heading: The Organic Act and Territorial Status
body: In 1900, Congress passed the Organic Act, formally establishing the Territory of Hawaiʻi with an American-style government structure, including a territorial legislature and a governor appointed by the U.S. president rather than elected locally, while extending U.S. citizenship to Hawaiian residents who had been citizens of the former Hawaiian Kingdom. Sanford Dole, who had led the Provisional Government and Republic of Hawaiʻi, became the first territorial governor.

Territorial status placed Hawaiʻi in a distinct legal middle ground: subject to U.S. federal law and represented in Congress only by a non-voting delegate, without full state representation or the constitutional protections statehood would eventually bring, an arrangement that lasted for nearly six decades until Hawaiʻi's admission to the Union in 1959.

example.problem: Explain why Congress used a joint resolution (the Newlands Resolution) rather than a ratified treaty to annex Hawaiʻi in 1898, and why this choice is still viewed as legally significant today.
steps: A formal treaty of annexation requires a two-thirds majority vote in the Senate, and earlier annexation treaty attempts had already failed to secure that supermajority, partly due to the well-documented Native Hawaiian opposition shown in the 1897 Kūʻē Petitions.

A joint resolution, by contrast, requires only a simple majority vote in both the House and Senate, a substantially lower bar that annexation supporters could reach even though a full treaty could not gain the needed two-thirds support.

Because the Constitution's treaty process, not a joint resolution, is the method explicitly described for the U.S. to enter binding international agreements, using a resolution instead to acquire foreign territory is viewed by some legal scholars and Native Hawaiian sovereignty advocates today as constitutionally questionable, a criticism that still shapes sovereignty debates in Hawaiʻi.
example.answer: Congress used the Newlands Resolution because it needed only simple majorities, letting annexation supporters bypass the two-thirds Senate vote that a formal treaty required and that documented Native Hawaiian opposition had already helped defeat, a procedural choice still viewed as constitutionally questionable by some scholars and sovereignty advocates today.

keyTerms.def: The July 1898 joint resolution, requiring only simple majorities, by which the U.S. formally annexed Hawaiʻi.
The law establishing the Territory of Hawaiʻi with a U.S.-style government and extending citizenship to Hawaiian residents.
Leader of the Provisional Government and Republic of Hawaiʻi, who became the first governor of the Territory of Hawaiʻi.

practice.q: Why did Congress use the Newlands Resolution instead of a formal treaty to annex Hawaiʻi?
choices: A treaty would have required unanimous approval from all 50 states
A joint resolution needed only simple majorities, unlike a treaty's required two-thirds Senate vote, which annexation had already failed to reach
The Newlands Resolution was proposed by Queen Liliʻuokalani herself
Treaties were illegal under U.S. law at the time
practice.explain: Earlier annexation treaties failed to gain the two-thirds Senate majority required, so Congress instead used a joint resolution, which needed only simple majorities in the House and Senate, to annex Hawaiʻi in 1898.

practice.q: What did the 1900 Organic Act establish?
choices: Full U.S. statehood for Hawaiʻi
The Territory of Hawaiʻi, with an American-style government and extended U.S. citizenship for Hawaiian residents
A return to the Hawaiian monarchy
Hawaiian independence from the United States
practice.explain: The Organic Act formally created the Territory of Hawaiʻi, establishing a territorial government structure and extending U.S. citizenship to residents who had been Hawaiian Kingdom citizens.

practice.q: Who became the first governor of the Territory of Hawaiʻi?
choices: Queen Liliʻuokalani
Sanford Dole, former leader of the Provisional Government and Republic of Hawaiʻi
John L. Stevens
Kamehameha III
practice.explain: Sanford Dole, who had led the Provisional Government and later the Republic of Hawaiʻi, was appointed the first governor of the newly established Territory of Hawaiʻi.

practice.q: Why do some scholars and sovereignty advocates still question the legality of the Newlands Resolution?
choices: Because it required a unanimous vote that was never obtained
Because the Constitution's explicit treaty process, not a joint resolution, is the method described for binding international agreements like acquiring foreign territory
Because it was signed by a Hawaiian monarch
Because it granted Hawaiʻi immediate statehood
practice.explain: Because the Constitution describes the treaty process for entering binding international agreements, using a joint resolution requiring only simple majorities to acquire foreign territory is viewed by some as a constitutionally questionable shortcut, a criticism still relevant to sovereignty debates today.

units.title: Hawaiʻi in the Twentieth Century
units.summary: Plantation immigration, the attack on Pearl Harbor, and the path to statehood transformed Hawaiʻi's population and political status over the course of the century.

lessons.title: Plantation Society and Immigration
lessons.intro: To keep sugar and pineapple plantations profitable, Hawaiʻi's planters recruited laborers from across the globe in waves, and those workers, thrown together from different countries with no shared language, built an entirely new hybrid language of their own to communicate on the job.

sections.heading: Waves of Plantation Labor
body: As sugar (and later pineapple) plantations expanded rapidly after the 1875 Reciprocity Treaty, planters recruited large numbers of contract laborers from abroad since the Native Hawaiian population, severely reduced by introduced diseases following Western contact, could not supply enough workers on its own. Major waves included Chinese laborers starting in the 1850s, Japanese laborers arriving in especially large numbers after 1885, and later Portuguese, Filipino, Korean, and Puerto Rican workers, each group recruited under multi-year labor contracts with often harsh working conditions.

By the early 20th century, this recruitment had transformed Hawaiʻi's population into one of the most ethnically diverse in the United States, with no single group forming an outright majority, a demographic pattern that distinguishes Hawaiʻi from most of the mainland United States to this day.

sections.heading: Pidgin: A New Language on the Plantation
body: Workers from China, Japan, the Philippines, Portugal, and elsewhere needed a shared way to communicate with each other and with English-speaking overseers despite having no common native language, and out of this necessity, Hawaiʻi Pidgin (more formally, Hawaiian Pidgin English or Hawaiʻi Creole English) developed on the plantations, blending vocabulary and grammatical patterns from English, Hawaiian, Portuguese, Japanese, and Cantonese and Filipino languages.

What began as a practical, simplified contact language between plantation workers gradually became a full, complex creole language, with its own stable grammar, spoken as a first language by later generations born in Hawaiʻi, and pidgin remains widely spoken and a genuine marker of local Hawaiʻi identity today, even as it has sometimes faced stigma in formal education and professional settings.

example.problem: Explain the linguistic process by which a practical, simplified communication tool used among plantation workers with no common language developed into Hawaiʻi Pidgin, a full creole language with its own stable grammar.
steps: Workers from many different language backgrounds, Chinese, Japanese, Filipino, Portuguese, and English-speaking overseers, needed a shared way to communicate on plantations despite having no common native language among them.

This necessity first produced a simplified contact language (sometimes called a pidgin in the linguistic sense), borrowing vocabulary and simplified grammatical patterns from each of these source languages to meet immediate, practical communication needs.

As children born on the plantations grew up hearing this contact language regularly and eventually learned it as their first language, it naturally developed the fuller, more stable, and more complex grammatical structure that defines a true creole language, which is the linguistic process that produced modern Hawaiʻi Pidgin.
example.answer: A practical contact language first emerged from the need for plantation workers of many backgrounds to communicate, and it developed into a full creole language, Hawaiʻi Pidgin, once children born in Hawaiʻi began learning it as their first, native language with its own stable grammar.

keyTerms.def: The multi-year labor agreements under which Hawaiian plantations recruited immigrant workers, often under harsh conditions.
A creole language that developed on Hawaiian plantations, blending English, Hawaiian, and immigrant languages.
A stable, fully grammatical language that develops from a simplified contact language once children learn it as a first language.

practice.q: Why did Hawaiian plantations recruit large numbers of foreign contract laborers?
choices: To replace an already large Native Hawaiian workforce
Because the Native Hawaiian population, reduced by introduced diseases, could not supply enough workers on its own
To comply with a U.S. federal mandate
Because Native Hawaiians refused to farm sugar
practice.explain: The Native Hawaiian population had been severely reduced by diseases introduced after Western contact, so planters recruited large numbers of foreign contract laborers, including Chinese, Japanese, Portuguese, and Filipino workers, to meet labor demands.

practice.q: What is Hawaiʻi Pidgin?
choices: The original Hawaiian language spoken before Western contact
A creole language that developed on plantations, blending English, Hawaiian, and immigrant languages
A formal legal language used only in government documents
A dialect spoken exclusively by tourists
practice.explain: Hawaiʻi Pidgin developed among plantation workers with no shared language, blending vocabulary and grammar from English, Hawaiian, Portuguese, Japanese, Cantonese, and Filipino languages into a distinct creole.

practice.q: What linguistic step turned Hawaiʻi Pidgin into a full creole language?
choices: Formal government legislation
Children born in Hawaiʻi learning it as their first native language, giving it stable, complex grammar
Its adoption as the sole language of instruction in schools
Translation of English textbooks into pidgin
practice.explain: A pidgin becomes a creole when children learn it as their first language, developing it into a fuller, more complex, and stable grammatical system, which is exactly what happened as generations grew up on Hawaiian plantations.

practice.q: What made Hawaiʻi's population distinctive by the early 20th century?
choices: It had one of the least diverse populations in the U.S.
It had become one of the most ethnically diverse populations in the U.S., with no single majority group
It consisted entirely of Native Hawaiians
It banned all forms of immigration
practice.explain: Waves of contract labor recruitment from China, Japan, the Philippines, Portugal, and elsewhere made Hawaiʻi's population highly diverse, with no single ethnic group forming a majority.

lessons.title: Pearl Harbor and Hawaiʻi in World War II
lessons.intro: In under two hours on a quiet Sunday morning, a surprise Japanese attack on Hawaiʻi's largest naval base pulled the United States directly into World War II and, almost overnight, subjected the entire territory to martial law under direct military rule.

sections.heading: The Attack on Pearl Harbor
body: On December 7, 1941, Japanese aircraft launched a surprise attack on the U.S. Pacific Fleet stationed at Pearl Harbor on Oʻahu, sinking or damaging numerous battleships, including the USS Arizona, whose sunken wreck still holds the remains of many of its crew and today serves as a national memorial, and killing over 2,300 American service members. The attack immediately brought the United States into World War II, with Congress declaring war on Japan the following day.

In the attack's immediate aftermath, the territorial governor declared martial law across Hawaiʻi, suspending civilian courts and constitutional protections and placing the territory under direct U.S. Army command for much of the war, an unusually severe and long-lasting military control not applied to the mainland United States.

sections.heading: Japanese American Hawaiʻi and the 442nd Regimental Combat Team
body: Unlike on the U.S. mainland, where the government forcibly removed and incarcerated most Japanese Americans, Hawaiʻi's territorial government did not mass-incarcerate its large Japanese American population (roughly a third of the islands' total population at the time), largely because doing so would have devastated the local economy and labor force the military itself depended on, though several thousand individuals deemed higher risk were still detained.

Thousands of Japanese American men from Hawaiʻi volunteered to serve, forming the core of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, which fought with distinction in Europe and became, for its size and length of service, one of the most decorated units in U.S. military history, a record its soldiers hoped, and largely succeeded, in using to prove their loyalty and challenge prejudice against Japanese Americans.

example.problem: Explain why Hawaiʻi's territorial government, unlike the mainland United States, did not mass-incarcerate its Japanese American population after Pearl Harbor, even though both were officially at war with Japan.
steps: Japanese Americans made up roughly a third of Hawaiʻi's total population at the time, a far larger share than on the mainland, where Japanese Americans were a small minority of the overall population.

Because Hawaiʻi's economy and essential labor force depended so heavily on this same population, mass incarceration would have crippled agriculture, construction, and other industries the military itself relied on to support the war effort in the Pacific.

This practical economic and logistical dependence, not any difference in official wartime policy toward Japanese Americans in general, is what led Hawaiian authorities to avoid mass incarceration, even while several thousand individuals considered higher risk were still detained.
example.answer: Because Japanese Americans made up roughly a third of Hawaiʻi's population and were essential to its labor force and wartime economy, mass incarceration would have crippled the islands' ability to function, leading authorities to avoid it even though a smaller number of individuals were still detained.

keyTerms.def: The U.S. Pacific Fleet's Oʻahu naval base, attacked by Japan on December 7, 1941, bringing the U.S. into World War II.
A battleship sunk during the Pearl Harbor attack, its wreck now serving as a national memorial to its lost crew.
Direct military rule suspending civilian courts and constitutional protections, declared in Hawaiʻi after Pearl Harbor.
A U.S. Army unit of Japanese American volunteers, including many from Hawaiʻi, that became one of the most decorated units in U.S. military history.

practice.q: What happened at Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941?
choices: The U.S. launched a surprise attack on Japan
Japan launched a surprise attack on the U.S. Pacific Fleet, bringing the U.S. into World War II
Hawaiʻi declared independence from the United States
A peace treaty was signed ending World War II
practice.explain: Japan's surprise attack on the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, killed over 2,300 service members and led Congress to declare war on Japan the following day, bringing the U.S. into World War II.

practice.q: What was declared in Hawaiʻi immediately after the Pearl Harbor attack?
choices: Statehood
Martial law, suspending civilian courts and placing the territory under Army command
Hawaiian independence
A new Hawaiian constitution
practice.explain: The territorial governor declared martial law across Hawaiʻi following the attack, suspending civilian courts and constitutional protections under direct U.S. Army command for much of the war.

practice.q: Why did Hawaiʻi's government not mass-incarcerate its Japanese American population as the mainland did?
choices: Hawaiʻi had no Japanese American residents
Japanese Americans made up roughly a third of Hawaiʻi's population and were essential to its labor force and economy
Federal law explicitly prohibited it in Hawaiʻi
The Japanese American population volunteered to be incarcerated
practice.explain: Because Japanese Americans formed such a large share of Hawaiʻi's population and workforce, mass incarceration would have crippled the territory's economy, leading authorities to avoid it despite detaining several thousand individuals considered higher risk.

practice.q: What was the 442nd Regimental Combat Team known for?
choices: Guarding Pearl Harbor exclusively
Becoming one of the most decorated units in U.S. military history despite its size
Refusing to fight in Europe
Being composed entirely of mainland soldiers
practice.explain: Composed largely of Japanese American volunteers from Hawaiʻi, the 442nd fought with distinction in Europe and became one of the most decorated units in U.S. military history relative to its size and length of service.

lessons.title: Statehood
lessons.intro: After six decades as a U.S. territory with no voting representation in Congress, Hawaiʻi's residents voted overwhelmingly in 1959 to become the fiftieth state, a decision that finally granted the islands full political rights within the country that had annexed them six decades earlier.

sections.heading: The Long Road to Statehood
body: Hawaiʻi's push for statehood began decades before it succeeded, but was repeatedly delayed in Congress by a mix of racial prejudice against Hawaiʻi's diverse, majority non-white population, concerns from some mainland politicians about labor union strength on the islands, and lingering distrust following the martial law period and wartime security concerns tied to Hawaiʻi's large Japanese American population.

Momentum shifted decisively after World War II, as the 442nd Regimental Combat Team's celebrated wartime record undercut arguments about Japanese American loyalty, and Cold War-era concerns about U.S. credibility on racial equality, especially while competing globally against Soviet propaganda, added political pressure to finally grant statehood to a racially diverse territory.

sections.heading: The 1959 Vote and Admission
body: Congress passed the Admission Act in March 1959, and in a subsequent June 1959 referendum, Hawaiʻi's registered voters approved statehood by an overwhelming margin, roughly 94 percent in favor, though critics, including some Native Hawaiian sovereignty advocates today, note the ballot offered no option to reject both statehood and existing territorial status in favor of restoring Hawaiian independence.

On August 21, 1959, Hawaiʻi officially became the 50th U.S. state, gaining full voting representation in Congress and the complete constitutional protections of statehood, a status that ended the unusual, decades-long territorial limbo that had followed the 1898 annexation and 1900 Organic Act.

example.problem: Explain why some Native Hawaiian sovereignty advocates today view the 1959 statehood vote as an incomplete or flawed exercise of self-determination, even though it passed by an overwhelming margin.
steps: The 1959 referendum offered voters a choice only between remaining a U.S. territory or becoming a U.S. state, both options that kept Hawaiʻi under U.S. control in some form.

The ballot did not include an option to restore full Hawaiian independence, the political status that existed before the 1893 overthrow and 1898 annexation many Native Hawaiians had opposed at the time, including in the 1897 Kūʻē Petitions.

Because voters were never given the choice to reject U.S. sovereignty over Hawaiʻi entirely, critics argue the 94 percent statehood result reflects a choice between two U.S.-controlled options rather than a genuine, complete exercise of self-determination that included independence as a possibility.
example.answer: Because the 1959 ballot only offered a choice between remaining a territory or becoming a state, both under U.S. sovereignty, and never offered restoring full independence as an option, some sovereignty advocates argue the vote did not represent a genuinely complete exercise of Hawaiian self-determination.

keyTerms.def: The March 1959 law authorizing Hawaiʻi's path to statehood, followed by a June 1959 statehood referendum.
The June 1959 vote in which Hawaiian residents approved statehood by roughly 94 percent.

practice.q: What factors delayed Hawaiian statehood for decades before 1959?
choices: A lack of interest from Hawaiian residents
Racial prejudice, labor union concerns, and distrust tied to the martial law period and Japanese American population
Opposition from the Hawaiian monarchy
A shortage of U.S. states available to admit Hawaiʻi
practice.explain: Statehood was repeatedly delayed by racial prejudice against Hawaiʻi's diverse population, concerns about labor union strength, and lingering wartime-era distrust, despite decades of local efforts to achieve it.

practice.q: What helped shift momentum toward statehood after World War II?
choices: The end of the sugar industry
The 442nd Regimental Combat Team's celebrated record and Cold War concerns about U.S. racial credibility
A new Hawaiian constitution
The Great Māhele land reforms
practice.explain: The celebrated wartime record of the 442nd undercut prejudice against Japanese Americans, and Cold War-era pressure to demonstrate U.S. racial equality on the world stage added momentum toward finally granting statehood.

practice.q: By roughly what margin did Hawaiian voters approve statehood in the 1959 referendum?
choices: About 50 percent
About 94 percent
About 25 percent
The referendum failed to pass
practice.explain: Hawaiian voters approved statehood by an overwhelming margin of roughly 94 percent in the June 1959 referendum, and Hawaiʻi officially became the 50th state on August 21, 1959.

practice.q: Why do some sovereignty advocates view the 1959 statehood vote as an incomplete exercise of self-determination?
choices: Because the vote was rigged by foreign powers
Because the ballot only offered statehood or continued territorial status, never full independence
Because too few residents voted
Because Congress overturned the results
practice.explain: The 1959 ballot offered no option to restore full Hawaiian independence, only a choice between two forms of continued U.S. control, which critics argue makes the result an incomplete measure of genuine self-determination.

units.title: The Wider Pacific and Contemporary Hawaiʻi
units.summary: How colonialism shaped other Pacific Island nations, how Hawaiian culture and language experienced a modern revival, and what sovereignty questions remain unresolved in Hawaiʻi today.

lessons.title: Colonialism Across the Pacific Islands
lessons.intro: Hawaiʻi's path from independent kingdom to U.S. territory to state was not unique in the Pacific, but the specific colonial powers involved, and how firmly or loosely each held on, varied enormously from island group to island group, producing a wide range of political arrangements that still exist today.

sections.heading: Melanesia and Polynesia Under Colonial Rule
body: Fiji became a British colony in 1874 after local chiefs ceded sovereignty, and Britain later brought large numbers of indentured Indian laborers to work Fijian sugar plantations, creating a lasting ethnic Indo-Fijian population and political tensions that persist in Fijian politics today; Fiji gained independence in 1970. Samoa was divided between colonial powers in 1899, with Germany taking the western islands (independent since 1962, the first Pacific Island nation to gain independence after World War II) and the United States retaining the eastern islands as American Samoa, still a U.S. territory today.

Tonga stands out as the only Pacific Island nation never fully colonized, having accepted British protection over its foreign affairs from 1900 to 1970 while retaining internal self-government and its monarchy throughout, a notably different outcome from Hawaiʻi's complete loss of sovereignty.

sections.heading: Micronesia and the Legacy of Shifting Colonial Powers
body: Guam, home to the Indigenous Chamorro people, became a Spanish colony and then passed to the United States after the 1898 Spanish-American War, the same conflict that helped drive U.S. interest in annexing Hawaiʻi; Guam remains an unincorporated U.S. territory today, and Chamorros gained U.S. citizenship through the Organic Act of Guam in 1950. Other Micronesian islands passed from Spanish to German to Japanese control before World War II and then became a United Nations Trust Territory administered by the United States afterward.

From that U.S.-administered trust territory, the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, and Palau eventually became independent nations, each entering a Compact of Free Association with the United States, an arrangement granting the U.S. certain military basing rights and providing these nations financial assistance in exchange, while their citizens retain the right to live and work in the United States without a visa.

example.problem: Compare Tonga's colonial history to Hawaiʻi's, and explain the key structural difference that let Tonga retain its monarchy and internal self-government while Hawaiʻi lost its monarchy entirely.
steps: Hawaiʻi's monarchy was physically overthrown in 1893 by an internal group of resident businessmen supported by landed U.S. Marines, followed by outright annexation as U.S. territory in 1898, a complete loss of sovereign political control.

Tonga, by contrast, accepted a more limited arrangement: Britain controlled only Tonga's foreign affairs starting in 1900, while the Tongan monarchy and Tongan officials retained full authority over the kingdom's internal governance throughout the entire period of British protection.

Because Tonga's arrangement never involved an internal overthrow of its monarchy or a formal transfer of full sovereignty to a colonial power the way Hawaiʻi's did, Tonga could resume full independent control in 1970 without needing to fully rebuild a monarchy or internal government system that had never actually been dismantled.
example.answer: Unlike Hawaiʻi, whose monarchy was overthrown and whose sovereignty was fully transferred through annexation, Tonga only ceded control of foreign affairs to Britain while keeping its monarchy and internal government intact throughout, which is why Tonga could resume full independence in 1970 without ever losing its core political institutions.

keyTerms.def: A Pacific nation that became a British colony in 1874 and gained independence in 1970, with a lasting Indo-Fijian population from colonial-era indentured labor.
The eastern Samoan islands retained by the United States after an 1899 division of Samoa with Germany, still a U.S. territory today.
The only Pacific Island nation never fully colonized, having accepted British control of foreign affairs while retaining its monarchy and self-government.
An agreement between the U.S. and Pacific nations like the Marshall Islands, granting the U.S. military access in exchange for aid and residency rights for citizens.

practice.q: What made Tonga's colonial experience different from Hawaiʻi's?
choices: Tonga was never in contact with any colonial power
Tonga ceded only foreign affairs control to Britain while keeping its monarchy and internal self-government intact
Tonga's monarchy was overthrown just like Hawaiʻi's
Tonga became a full British colony with no self-government
practice.explain: Unlike Hawaiʻi, whose monarchy was overthrown and sovereignty fully transferred, Tonga retained its monarchy and internal governance throughout, ceding only control of foreign affairs to Britain from 1900 to 1970.

practice.q: How was Samoa divided among colonial powers in 1899?
choices: Germany took the eastern islands and the U.S. took the western islands
Germany took the western islands and the United States took the eastern islands (American Samoa)
Britain took all of Samoa
Samoa was never divided by any colonial power
practice.explain: The 1899 division gave Germany the western Samoan islands, which became independent in 1962, while the United States retained the eastern islands as American Samoa, still a U.S. territory today.

practice.q: What is a Compact of Free Association?
choices: A military alliance requiring mandatory conscription
An agreement granting the U.S. military basing rights in exchange for aid and residency rights for citizens of nations like the Marshall Islands
A trade agreement exclusive to Guam
A historical treaty that ended Spanish colonization
practice.explain: The Compact of Free Association links the U.S. with former trust territories like the Marshall Islands, Federated States of Micronesia, and Palau, granting the U.S. military access while providing aid and U.S. residency rights to their citizens.

practice.q: How did Guam come under U.S. control?
choices: Through voluntary annexation by Guam's legislature
It passed to the U.S. from Spain after the 1898 Spanish-American War
Guam was purchased directly from the Chamorro people
It was granted independence and then rejoined the U.S.
practice.explain: Guam passed from Spanish to U.S. control after the 1898 Spanish-American War, the same conflict that helped drive U.S. strategic interest in annexing Hawaiʻi, and remains an unincorporated U.S. territory today.

lessons.title: The Hawaiian Renaissance
lessons.intro: By the 1970s, the Hawaiian language was in steep decline, spoken fluently by only a small and aging number of Native Hawaiians, but a wave of cultural pride and activism, sparked partly by a single voyaging canoe, reversed decades of suppression and brought hula, chant, and ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi back into everyday Hawaiian life.

sections.heading: From Suppression to Revival
body: Following annexation, the Hawaiian language was formally banned as a language of instruction in public schools starting in 1896, a policy that, combined with broader social and economic pressure to assimilate into English-speaking American life, caused a steep, multi-generational decline in the number of fluent Native Hawaiian speakers by the mid-20th century. Traditional hula also faced decades of missionary-era suppression and later commercialization for tourism that stripped much of its original cultural and spiritual depth.

Beginning in the late 1960s and accelerating through the 1970s, a broad cultural movement historians call the Hawaiian Renaissance emerged, driven by a new generation of Native Hawaiians reclaiming language, hula, chant, and traditional practices as sources of pride and identity rather than something to abandon.

sections.heading: Hōkūleʻa's Role and Language Revitalization
body: The 1976 voyage of Hōkūleʻa, discussed earlier for its navigational significance, also became a powerful symbol of the Hawaiian Renaissance more broadly, demonstrating Native Hawaiian ingenuity and connecting contemporary Hawaiians directly to their voyaging ancestors at a moment when cultural pride was surging. Hula also underwent a serious revival, with institutions like the annual Merrie Monarch Festival, founded in 1971 and named for King Kalākaua, helping restore hula's status as a rigorously trained, respected art form rather than mere tourist entertainment.

Language revitalization became a central, urgent priority as it became clear fluent Hawaiian speakers were aging and few children were learning ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi as a first language; this led to the founding of Pūnana Leo Hawaiian-language immersion preschools starting in 1984 and the expansion of full Hawaiian-language immersion education (kula kaiapuni) through later grades, a program credited with raising a new generation of fluent young Hawaiian speakers for the first time in decades.

example.problem: Explain why Hawaiian language immersion preschools, rather than simply offering Hawaiian language classes to older students, were seen as the most urgent and effective response to the near-total loss of Native Hawaiian speakers by the 1980s.
steps: By the 1980s, most fluent Native Hawaiian speakers were elderly, and very few children anywhere were learning ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi as their first language in the home, meaning the language risked losing its last generation of natural speakers within a matter of decades.

Learning a language as a young child through full immersion produces a much deeper, more natural fluency than studying it later in life as an academic subject, since young children acquire language most readily and thoroughly during early childhood.

By starting immersion at the preschool level with Pūnana Leo, educators aimed to raise an entirely new generation of genuinely fluent first-language Hawaiian speakers from early childhood onward, addressing the urgency of the language's decline more directly than classroom instruction for older students alone could.
example.answer: Because fluent speakers were aging and almost no children were learning Hawaiian as a first language, starting full immersion at the preschool level through Pūnana Leo aimed to raise a genuinely fluent new generation from early childhood, addressing the urgent risk of the language's near-total loss more effectively than later classroom instruction could.

keyTerms.def: A cultural revival movement beginning in the late 1960s and 1970s reclaiming Hawaiian language, hula, and traditional practices.
An annual hula competition and festival founded in 1971, named for King Kalākaua, that helped restore hula's respected status.
Hawaiian-language immersion preschools founded starting in 1984 to raise a new generation of fluent Hawaiian speakers.
Hawaiian-language immersion education extended through later grades, building on the Pūnana Leo preschool model.

practice.q: What 1896 policy contributed to the steep decline of the Hawaiian language?
choices: A law requiring all schools to teach only Hawaiian
A ban on Hawaiian as a language of instruction in public schools
The founding of Pūnana Leo preschools
The Great Māhele land reforms
practice.explain: The 1896 ban on Hawaiian as a language of instruction in public schools, combined with broader assimilation pressure, drove a steep, multi-generational decline in fluent Hawaiian speakers by the mid-20th century.

practice.q: What broader cultural movement emerged in Hawaiʻi beginning in the late 1960s and 1970s?
choices: The Bayonet Constitution movement
The Hawaiian Renaissance, reclaiming language, hula, and traditional practices
The Great Māhele
The Kūʻē Petition movement
practice.explain: The Hawaiian Renaissance was a cultural revival movement in which a new generation of Native Hawaiians reclaimed language, hula, chant, and traditional practices as sources of pride rather than things to abandon.

practice.q: Why did Pūnana Leo focus specifically on preschool-age immersion rather than only teaching Hawaiian to older students?
choices: Because older students were legally barred from learning Hawaiian
Because young children acquire language most naturally and thoroughly, offering the best path to raising genuinely fluent new speakers
Because preschools required less funding than other schools
Because Hawaiian could only legally be taught before age five
practice.explain: Because fluent speakers were aging and almost no children were learning Hawaiian as a first language, full immersion starting at the preschool level aimed to build genuine fluency from early childhood, when language acquisition is most natural and effective.

practice.q: What role did the Merrie Monarch Festival play in the Hawaiian Renaissance?
choices: It banned hula from being performed publicly
It helped restore hula's status as a rigorously trained, respected art form rather than tourist entertainment
It focused exclusively on Hawaiian language classes
It was founded to promote statehood
practice.explain: Founded in 1971 and named for King Kalākaua, the Merrie Monarch Festival became a major venue helping restore hula's reputation as a serious, disciplined art form during the Hawaiian Renaissance.

lessons.title: Sovereignty and Hawaiʻi Today
lessons.intro: A century after the overthrow, the United States government formally apologized for its role in ending the Hawaiian Kingdom, yet that apology raised as many questions as it answered about what, if anything, should follow, questions that remain very much alive in Hawaiʻi's politics today.

sections.heading: The 1993 Apology Resolution
body: In 1993, on the one-hundredth anniversary of the overthrow, the U.S. Congress passed and President Bill Clinton signed the Apology Resolution, a joint resolution formally acknowledging that the overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom had been illegal and that Native Hawaiians never directly relinquished their claims to sovereignty over Hawaiian lands or their national identity. The resolution, however, was explicitly symbolic and created no legal mechanism for returning land, restoring the monarchy, or establishing any new Native Hawaiian government.

The Apology Resolution nonetheless gave renewed legal and political weight to the modern Hawaiian sovereignty movement, a broad and internally diverse set of groups holding differing goals ranging from full restoration of an independent Hawaiian nation to a federally recognized Native Hawaiian governing entity similar to those of many Native American tribes, to more limited forms of cultural and land-based redress within the existing state government.

sections.heading: Ongoing Sovereignty and Land Issues
body: Contemporary sovereignty debates connect directly to unresolved issues from the Great Māhele and annexation, including the roughly 1.8 million acres of former crown and government land that passed to the state of Hawaiʻi at statehood, land that some Native Hawaiian groups argue should be held in trust or returned rather than treated as ordinary state property. The Office of Hawaiian Affairs, established by the state in 1978, currently manages certain programs and revenues intended to benefit Native Hawaiians as part of this unresolved land legacy.

Land and cultural issues have also produced high-profile modern conflicts, most notably the sustained protests over the proposed Thirty Meter Telescope on Mauna Kea, a mountain many Native Hawaiians consider profoundly sacred, where large demonstrations beginning in 2014 and intensifying in 2019 highlighted ongoing tensions between scientific development, land use, and Native Hawaiian cultural and religious rights that remain unresolved.

example.problem: Explain why the 1993 Apology Resolution, despite formally acknowledging the overthrow was illegal, did not by itself resolve Native Hawaiian sovereignty claims, and why this distinction matters for understanding today's ongoing sovereignty debates.
steps: The Apology Resolution was worded as a formal, symbolic acknowledgment of historical wrongdoing, explicitly without creating any binding legal mechanism to return land, restore the monarchy, or establish a new Native Hawaiian governing body.

Because the resolution changed no actual laws governing land ownership, political status, or governance, the practical situation regarding former crown and government lands and Native Hawaiian political status remained legally unchanged after 1993, even though the historical record had been formally corrected.

This gap between symbolic acknowledgment and concrete legal remedy is precisely why sovereignty movements continued and diversified after 1993, since acknowledging past wrongdoing did not itself settle the unresolved practical questions about land, governance, and Native Hawaiian political status that remain actively debated today.
example.answer: Because the Apology Resolution was explicitly symbolic and created no binding legal remedy for land or governance, it left the underlying practical sovereignty and land questions unresolved, which is exactly why sovereignty movements and debates over Hawaiian land and political status have continued and diversified in the decades since 1993.
